newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Fixing EMU conversion rates poses tricky problems.
newsitem.headline: Fixing EMU conversion rates poses tricky problems.

text.p: By standing ready to defend existing cross-rates among European currencies, EU governments can go a long way towards limiting currency instability ahead of the single currency's introduction, analysts say.

EU governments anxiously want to prevent market speculation from derailing the euro during the period after the decision on which countries will participate, expected in early May 1998, and the launch date, January 1, 1999.
Luxembourg, which takes over the EU presidency in July, has said it will push quickly to set "indicative" exchange rates for national currencies against the single currency.

What is meant by "indicative" may be less than clear, but a growing number of experts say the most effective way to give markets stability ahead of 1999 is to reaffirm the central parity rates within Europe's Exchange Rate Mechanism.

A new study from the London-based Centre for Economic Policy Research (CEPR) goes into considerable detail over how this could come about and the limits EU policy-makers face in preventing unwanted currency speculation.
Specifically, commitments made under the Maastricht Treaty and at past EU summits have reduced the options in making early decisions on conversion rates. Three agreements stand out:
-- conversion rates between the euro and the national currencies of the participating countries will be decided at the beginning of 1999 (Maastricht Treaty);

-- at this time, the "external" value of the Ecu must not change (Maastricht Treaty). The CEPR report suggests that a proper reading of "external" means the exchange rate "against any currency including the currencies of all EMU participants."
-- the euro, being the legal extension of the Ecu, should convert initially at one for one with the Ecu (Madrid summit, December 1995).

The technical implications of these decisions imply that the conversion rates for EMU members cannot differ from those existing in the market on December 31, 1998 and therefore cannot be specified in advance.

"The rule that the Ecu will be converted to the euro one for one and the fact that the Ecu contains the currencies of countries that will not participate in EMU have a bizarre implication," the CEPR study notes.

"Giving markets complete certainty that EMU will not involve capital gains or losses on the last day makes it impossible to create any certainty about the conversion rates of the currencies participating in the euro any day before December 1998," the report added.

What the authors of the study recommend instead, and what appears to be within the legal parameters of Maastricht, is for EU leaders to fix bilateral exchange rates among EMU members ahead of the launch date.
Even if the participating countries are not known until early 1998, a decision that the existing central parities in the ERM will be used to fix the bilateral rates could be made early.
At the moment, there is a considerable degree of stability within the ERM, with most currencies -- apart from the Irish punt -- trading very close to their central parities.

"Such an announcement would not face the same credibilty problems as fixing exchange rates with outside currencies, because the central banks that will participate in EMU would only have to coordinate their monetary policies among themselves," the study said.
Because the Ecu is a basket of all EU member states, the difficulty of maintaining the Ecu's external value becomes the root of the problem.
EU monetary officials are likely to take up the issue of bilateral conversion rates in September at an informal meeting of finance ministers and central bankers in Luxembourg.
